terms.example: Meet your flight crew.

terms.what: Pip's signature trail of yellow bubbles.
terms.guidance: Cosmetic name; cute and short.

terms.what: Peaches's signature trail of little hearts.
terms.guidance: Peach-coloured hearts; the name echoes Peaches.

terms.what: Minty's signature trail of small mint leaves.
terms.guidance: Mint leaves; echoes Minty.

terms.what: Orbit's signature trail of stardust.
terms.guidance: Cosmetic name.

terms.what: Settings switch that turns off all spoken lines: story scenes, thank-you notes and sprint calls, and the flight talk.
terms.guidance: Settings label.

terms.what: Settings switch for the music ("Menu, adventure and boss themes.").
terms.guidance: Same "Sky Club" as ui.sky-club.

terms.what: Accessibility setting: quieter menus and fewer decorative effects.
terms.guidance: Use the platform's usual accessibility term.

terms.what: The campaign map: one stop per region with numbered level nodes on a dotted mail route; also the pause/result button "Map".
where: UI: "A postcard is waiting on the map!"
terms.guidance: Short button label.
terms.example: A postcard is waiting on the map!

terms.what: One region on the campaign map ("Previous stop", "Next stop"); also the narrator's "Next stop: Paris".
terms.guidance: A stop on a journey (like a bus/train stop). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: To be continued… Next stop: Paris, the City of Light.

terms.what: One of the five campaign routes ("CHAPTER 1 · THE CANOPY ROUTE", "Chapter 1 postcard").
terms.guidance: Book chapter.

terms.what: One campaign stage ("Level 1-1"), or a built level.
where: UI: map, level card, Level Builder ("My levels", "New level")
terms.guidance: Plain game word; level ids like 1-1 stay as digits.

terms.what: The card that opens over the map for a level: name, region, the SPECIAL DELIVERY cargo tag, hint, star targets, controls, Fly!
terms.guidance: Not printed; the card's parts are separate entries.

terms.what: The heading on the level card's parcel tag above the cargo; also the hidden achievement "Special Delivery" and a phrase in voice lines.
terms.guidance: The postal service term for an express/registered delivery; reuse it in the achievement (achievement.special-delivery) and the voice lines. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Special delivery: a sundial for the dawn keeper! Heavy, but punctual. Like me!

terms.what: The one-line hint on a level card, marked NEW when it introduces something; also Bill's tips quoted by the birds ("Bill's tip").
where: flight voice ("Just like the tip: chain the stars!")
terms.guidance: Short label. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Just like the tip: chain the stars! Chaining!

terms.what: The air-mail note that drops in on a finished level's result: the recipient's thanks in quotes, signed "— the toucan twins", read aloud in their voice. A beaten boss grumbles its thanks.
where: UI: settings ("Story scenes, thank-you notes and sprint calls.")
terms.guidance: A short thank-you card/note. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Every thank-you note boils down to one perfect drop!

terms.what: The illustrated postcard after each chapter's boss ("SKY CLUB POSTCARD", "Dear courier,", "Greetings from", "P.S."; addressed to "The courier / Sky Club post / Up in the sky"); and the daily Adventure card ("POSTCARD STAMPED!").
where: UI: results ("A postcard is waiting on the map!")
terms.guidance: Postcard; keep the letter conventions of your language for "Dear courier," and "P.S.".
terms.example: A postcard is waiting on the map!

terms.what: A chapter boss's level and map node (the last of the chapter): "the boss's lair".
where: UI: map (larger node with the boss's name)
docs, achievements ("Beat Baron Bat in his lair")
terms.guidance: A villain's den; Bill says it once ("His lair is just beyond those mountains."). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Red sun, red sky. His lair is just beyond those mountains.

terms.what: The word for a campaign mini-boss (Neferhoo, King Coo, the Searchlight Gargoyle) on its name card, map plaque, level card ribbon and result ("Guardian down!"). Never "mini-boss".
where: story (Bill: "No flame seal on this guardian.")
terms.guidance: One word everywhere, including Bill's spoken "guardian".
terms.example: No flame seal on this guardian. Just a very old, very stubborn postman.

terms.what: A big enemy fought at the end of a level or in endless ("BOSS FIGHT", "Boss down!", "Beat Baron Bat").
terms.guidance: Standard game word (often the loanword "boss"). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Another one? My notes only covered one boss!

terms.what: The small gold word above a chapter boss's name on its entrance card, numbered by boss order (ENCOUNTER 01 … 05).
terms.guidance: All caps, short, keep the two-digit number.

terms.what: A boss's entrance card: eyebrow (ENCOUNTER/GUARDIAN), name, epithet, and in the campaign its line in quotes.
terms.guidance: Not printed; its parts are separate entries (title.*, phrase.*-line).

terms.what: A boss's second stage: at 2/3 health it roars, a heart floats in and the bar tag reads "STRONGER · …".
where: UI: boss bar tag ("STRONGER!", "STRONGER · Triple shots, and his bats join in!")
terms.guidance: One short caps word.
terms.example: STRONGER!

terms.what: A boss's third stage (below 1/3 health): fiercer attacks ("FURY · Faster fireballs").
terms.guidance: One short caps word; the birds say "boss-mad" lines here ("Somebody's cranky now!").
terms.example: FURY · Express post and two ankhs

terms.what: The victory card title when a chapter's boss falls (a guardian's says GUARDIAN DOWN!).
terms.guidance: Triumphant, short, all caps.

terms.what: The victory card and result title when a guardian falls ("Guardian down!").
terms.guidance: Same "guardian" word as ui.guardian; same words on card and result.

terms.what: The result title for a beaten chapter boss.
terms.guidance: Short.

terms.what: The result title for a finished ordinary level; birds shout it too.
terms.guidance: Past participle of deliver (mail). Gender/number agreement may be needed in some languages: prefer a form that needs none. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Delivered! Signed, sealed, and exactly on time!

terms.what: The result title of a failed level.
terms.guidance: Short, encouraging.

terms.what: The knockout stage title when the bird loses its last heart in the sky ("A little bump in the clouds."); at sea it is "Splash!".
terms.guidance: Comic bump sound word; use your language's cartoon bump onomatopoeia. Not to be confused with the Empress's "Bonk. Bonk." (her moths hitting lamps), though the same sound word fits both. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Bonk. I'm okay. Writing that down as okay.

terms.what: The knockout stage title when the bird falls into the sea ("A little splash in the sea.").
terms.guidance: Comic water sound word. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Splash! Cold! Cold! Cold!

terms.what: On the knockout stage: how much of the level's route was flown ("N percent of the route flown").
where: UI: knockout stage, HUD ("Route N% flown")
terms.guidance: Same "route" word as the mail routes.

terms.what: Ribbon on locked map stops whose levels are not in this build (Paris and chapters 4–5); "Paris — coming soon".
terms.guidance: Short ribbon text.

terms.what: Lock notes on map nodes and keys ("Finish 1-2 to unlock", "Beat Baron Bat to unlock", "Unlocks in N flights", "Unlock Pip for N stars").
where: UI: map, level card, home keys, collection
terms.guidance: Standard game verb.

terms.what: The level card key that replays a level's scene; "Skip" ends a scene; "Next line" advances it.
terms.guidance: Short labels.

terms.what: The end card of a stop whose chapter is not finished (New York until Paris opens), read by the narrator.
terms.guidance: Use the usual TV/comic phrase in your language; keep the ellipsis character "…". The scene player detects this caption by its text, so tell the UI architect your exact wording. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: To be continued… Next stop: Paris, the City of Light.

terms.what: The pause card ("Take a breather.") with Map, Retry and Keep flying.
terms.guidance: Friendly pause title; button labels "Retry", "Keep flying", "Map".

terms.what: The basic control (tap to flap); a control label on the level card and in co-op ("FLAP SHARE", "P1 flaps").
terms.guidance: A wing beat; short verb.
terms.example: Tap to flap. Fly through the stars.

terms.what: The level card's start button; also "Fly again", "Fly with Pip", "FLY" in the builder.
where: UI: level card, results, collection, builder
terms.guidance: Short imperative.

terms.what: Lifetime push-ups, squats and jumps from the camera mini games and built levels ("WORKOUT", "Workouts · 2 players").
where: UI: records, builder result, home key
terms.guidance: Keep it light; mini games are a side feature.

terms.what: Setting up the camera mini games: the game learns the player's movement range ("CALIBRATING", "Calibrated! Try moving your bird.").
where: UI: mini game setup, camera lab
terms.guidance: Technical but friendly.
terms.example: Your bird moves after calibration.

terms.what: Settings entry to test body tracking.
terms.guidance: Settings label.

terms.what: Google Play Games: optional cloud save and achievements ("Connect Play Games", "Cloud save & achievements").
terms.guidance: Google's product name: use Google's own localized name for "Google Play Games" in each language (it is often kept in English). "Cloud save" and "achievements" are translated.
terms.example: Play Games achievements

terms.what: Google Play Games achievements (42), opened from Settings.
terms.guidance: Use Google Play's own term in your language.
terms.example: Cloud save & achievements

terms.what: A Level Builder level as a text code (BEAK1.…) to paste to a friend ("Share code", "Paste code", "Code copied! Paste it to a friend.").
terms.guidance: Short labels.
terms.example: Code copied! Paste it to a friend.

terms.what: Copying a starter or shared level to edit it as your own ("Remix it to make it yours").
terms.guidance: Loanword "remix" is fine where usual.
terms.example: Starter level · look, fly or remix

terms.what: The five read-only template levels in the builder ("look, fly or remix").
terms.guidance: Shelf title.
terms.example: Starter levels stay as they are: remix it to change it.

terms.what: The area at the start of a built level that must stay clear ("START ZONE · KEEP CLEAR").
terms.guidance: All caps, short.
terms.example: Keep the start zone clear: place things right of the dashed line.

terms.what: The kind of gate in the builder (Garden gate, Wind lift, Petal shutters, Switchback, Lantern drift, Sun wheels, Crystal steps): "How the gate looks and moves."
terms.guidance: A family/type of gate.

terms.what: A built level can end with a boss instead of a finish line ("waits at the end"); its place is the "boss mark".
terms.guidance: Short label.
terms.example: Boss mark: tap the sky to move where the boss waits

terms.what: A built level its maker has flown to the finish (needed to share it); a shared one says "Cleared by its maker".
terms.guidance: Short status.
terms.example: Cleared by you: you flew it to the end.

terms.what: A built level's speed: Relaxed, Steady, Brisk.
terms.guidance: Three short adjectives in rising order.

terms.what: The two heights a push-up/squat bird flies (top and bottom lane); also King Coo's "open lane" and the Dragon's "fire lane".
where: UI: King Coo fight ("OPEN LANE = GO")
terms.guidance: A track/lane. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Shoot him when he puffs up to whistle. Dodge stale crumb bombs, fly the open lane!

terms.what: The two players of Fly Together ("P1", "P2", "Player 1 wins!").
terms.guidance: Keep "P1"/"P2" short (or your usual abbreviation).
terms.example: Player 1 taps the left half to flap, player 2 the right half

terms.what: Co-op result: the shared score; "TEAM BEST", "NEW TEAM BEST!", "FLAP SHARE".
terms.guidance: All caps, short.

terms.what: Duel result button; "SERIES" counts wins; "A draw!".

terms.what: The wax seal shaped like a flame on the warm letters that told each boss its route was theirs to take; the trail of seals leads to the Ember Dragon. Guardians have none ("No flame seal on this guardian").
terms.guidance: A wax seal (on an envelope) in the shape of a flame; one fixed phrase. "seal" also alone ("Two routes, two seals."). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
aliases: a seal shaped like a flame
terms.example: And look what the Baron left behind: a scorched envelope with a flame seal.

terms.what: How each boss describes the Dragon's letter: literally warm (from a dragon) and kind in tone ("warm as toast").
terms.guidance: Double meaning: physically warm and friendly. Keep both if your language allows. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Did a warm letter tell you the road was yours?

terms.what: The post delivered at night in New York and Paris; it can't find a door while the lamps are dark. Also the hidden achievement "Night Mail".
terms.guidance: Night post/mail service; one fixed phrase. (English TTS in a whisper heard it as "nightmare".) Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Hush now. The night mail is sleeping.

terms.what: The dawn mail delivery that wakes Baron Bat ("My oldest, noisiest enemy").
where: flight voice (baron arrive; Minty "The morning post is here.")
terms.guidance: The morning mail round. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: He says the morning post wakes him. His bedtime is our rush hour.

terms.what: One of the Sky Club's five mail routes (each taken by a boss); route six is the new Edge of the Map route. Key word of the story ("Who would steal a mail route?").
terms.guidance: A postal delivery route (round). Use ONE word in chapter names, boss lines, Bill's lines and the HUD. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Who would steal a mail route?

terms.what: The new Sky Club route the Dragon will light: the Edge of the Map.
terms.guidance: Same "route" word; ordinal as natural. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Route six, Dragon: the Edge of the Map. You light it. We deliver it.

terms.what: The light at the edge of the map that the Dragon is invited to keep ("Come and keep our beacon.").
terms.guidance: A signal fire/lighthouse light; "keep" = tend. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: “Come and keep our beacon. Signed: everyone. Even the Baron.”

terms.what: The one letter the club ever lost in Egypt in four thousand years: Neferhoo's, addressed to the Sphinx, right outside the pyramid. "THE LOST LETTER IS FOUND" on his victory card.
terms.guidance: Ties to title.keeper-of-the-lost-letter.
terms.example: So that’s the letter we lost! The Sphinx was too polite to complain.

terms.what: The Sky Club's ledgers of deliveries ("I checked the books twice.").
terms.guidance: Account books / records. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Somebody who has never been sent a letter. I checked the books twice.

terms.what: The club's letter-sorting compartments; Bill's pun: "Our pigeonholes have never had a pigeon." He offers King Coo the job of their Commissioner.
terms.guidance: Pun: pigeonhole (mail sorting slot) + pigeon. Recreate with your word for mail slots/sorting boxes, and a joke about finally having a pigeon in them. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Our pigeonholes have never had a pigeon. Commissioner wanted. Pay: a hot bagel a day.

terms.what: King Coo's beloved bread cart, at the same corner every night; tonight it was gone, leaving only wheel tracks. It was sheltering from the rain under the theatre marquee.
where: UI: arrival line ("Somebody is very cross about the bread cart…")
terms.guidance: A street vendor's bread/bakery cart with wheels. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Nobody flies till the bread cart is found!

terms.what: King Coo's pay for his new club job.
terms.guidance: New York bagel; keep "bagel" if known, else a local bread roll. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: A bagel a day? …The Commissioner accepts.

terms.what: The Gargoyle's new job: shining the night mail home so every courier looks up.
terms.guidance: Aviation landing light. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Stoneface, the night mail needs a landing light. Every courier will look up!

terms.what: The Spitter King's potion of boiled letters for an ink that never fades; it ends up "all… minty" (mint tea).
terms.guidance: A potion/brew being boiled. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Every letter on my road goes in the brew!

terms.what: The Spitter King's goal: "The perfect ink. One that never fades." ("Bah. It was very nearly ink.").
terms.guidance: Ink. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: The perfect ink. One that never fades. I only needed a few thousand letters.

terms.what: What the Spitter King's brew turns into, and the club's allowed drink ("Tea is allowed."); Minty jokes it is named after him.
terms.guidance: Mint tea. Ties to Minty's name. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Brew's done, Your Majesty! Try mint tea. Named after me, basically.

terms.what: The Spitter King's recipe uses typical phrases from letters as ingredients ("One “Dear Grandma”, two “Wish you were here”, stir…"; "A pinch of Get Well Soon, a dash of Love From...").
terms.guidance: Replace with the stock phrases of letters and postcards in your language (greeting, "wish you were here", "get well soon", "love from"), keeping the recipe rhythm. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: But the recipe! One “Dear Grandma”, two “Wish you were here”, stir…

terms.what: POSTAGE stamps: the Pirate Captain's treasure ("Tiny paper treasure from every port!"); he keeps the envelopes and throws the letters back; the club will send him a stamp from every route.
terms.guidance: Postage stamps (fr timbres, de Briefmarken, ja 切手…), NOT the passport's ink stamps (ui.passport-stamp). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Not the mail, lad. The STAMPS. Tiny paper treasure from every port!

terms.what: The Pirate Captain's precious album, soggy after his defeat.
terms.guidance: A stamp collector's album. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Me hat! Me ship! Me stamp album… it’s soggy.

terms.what: The world's first adhesive postage stamp (UK, 1840), the rarest prize the Captain hopes for.
terms.guidance: Use the established philatelic name in your language (often kept as "Penny Black"); Pip's related fact: "the first stamp cost one penny". Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Word is, there's a penny black in that bag...

terms.what: What the Captain keeps (for their stamps) while throwing the letters back.
terms.guidance: Envelopes. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: That’s the odd part. He throws the letters back and keeps the envelopes.

terms.what: Baron Bat's reason for taking the route: he needs his beauty sleep and the dawn post wakes him.
terms.guidance: Idiom for the sleep that keeps you beautiful. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Every dawn: flap, thump, “POST!” A bat needs his beauty sleep.

terms.what: The deal with Baron Bat: the canopy is delivered at dusk, not dawn ("Dusk! How civilised.").
terms.guidance: Dusk = evening twilight (same "dusk" word as the Dusk Empress is fine). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Oh, fine. Deliver at dusk, like civilised birds.

terms.what: The city street lamps the Dusk Empress put to sleep so her moths would stop bumping into them; in the end they get shades and she lights them each dusk.
terms.guidance: Street lamps. English TTS misheard "lamps" as "lambs" (it is pinned with IPA /læmps/ in the English prompt only); check your language's word is not a near-homophone in the take. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Shh. You will wake the lamps.

terms.what: The courier's gentle solution for the Empress's moths ("We could just add lampshades…", "Shades… Yes.").
terms.guidance: Lamp shades; the Empress shortens it to "Shades…". Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: About those lampshades. Soft ones. Would they help?

terms.what: Bells that ring when the post comes in to port; silent while the Captain raids the mail.
terms.guidance: Port bells. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: The tide route. Harbour bells ring when the post comes in. None has rung all week.

terms.what: Bill's phrase introducing the motto ("Club rule: every letter lands."); Pip: "Rule one: be polite."
terms.guidance: The club's rule. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Start small: one birthday card, one jungle. Club rule: every letter lands.

terms.what: The formal last warning letter the courier hands Baron Bat ("Final notice. You're roosting on a mail route.").
terms.guidance: Official "final notice" (bill/eviction style). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Final notice. You’re roosting on a mail route.

terms.what: Cargo 3-8 for the Dusk Empress; also the Baron's "Consider that your wake-up call." Literal (alarm) and figurative (warning).
terms.guidance: Keep both meanings if possible. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Singed? Consider that your wake-up call.

terms.term: the first letter ever sent to the Dragon
terms.what: The last delivery: a letter signed by everyone, the beaten bosses included ("Even the Baron. He dotted his “i” with a tiny bat."), inviting the Dragon to keep the beacon.
terms.guidance: The payoff of the story; the letter itself is read aloud in Bill's voice. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: I have the letter. Everybody signed it.

terms.term: He dotted his “i” with a tiny bat.
terms.what: Bill's joke: the Baron signed the letter and drew a tiny bat as the dot on his i.
terms.guidance: Depends on the letter "i" having a dot; if your script has none, adapt (e.g. a tiny bat drawn by his signature). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Even the Baron. He dotted his “i” with a tiny bat.

terms.what: The courier's bag of letters (and the Captain's target: "Every mailbag on these waves be mine!"); Bill's pouch was the club's first mailbag.
terms.guidance: Postal bag. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Arr! Every mailbag on these waves be mine!

terms.what: Neferhoo's courier satchel "full of letters nobody wanted".
terms.guidance: Shoulder bag; can be the same as mailbag. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: My satchel is full of letters nobody wanted. Take one!

terms.what: Ancient Egypt's royal mail service that Neferhoo flew for ("No courier flies the Pharaoh's post but me!").
terms.guidance: Same "post" word as ui.sky-club-post. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: HALT! No courier flies the Pharaoh’s post but me!

terms.what: Neferhoo's golden mask of the Pharaoh's post; it hid the letter's door from him; when it comes off he can see ("My mask! …Oh. Oh my. I can see!").
terms.guidance: A golden (funeral) mask. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: My mask! …Oh. Oh my. I can see!

terms.what: Neferhoo's linen mummy wraps ("Rocks only scuff his wraps. Shoot his LETTERS back!").
where: flight voice ("You have crumpled my wrappings!")
terms.guidance: Mummy bandages. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: You have crumpled my wrappings!

terms.what: What each boss loses when beaten and what its stamp shows: Baron Bat's crown ("It always pinched"), the Spitter King's flask crown (kept as a vase), the Empress's diadem, the Captain's hat, King Coo's police cap, the Gargoyle's brow visor, Neferhoo's golden mask.
terms.guidance: Translate each item plainly; "flask crown" = a crown made of a laboratory flask. The Empress calls her diadem "my crown" in the story ("My crown has slipped.") and "diadem" in flight; follow each line. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: My crown! …Oh, keep it. It always pinched.

terms.what: Small wood for starting a fire: the Dragon says letters are kindling.
terms.guidance: Firewood/tinder. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: The sky is mine. Your letters are kindling.

terms.what: Bill's quip: the Baron's bedtime is the post's rush hour.
terms.guidance: Idiom for the busiest commuting hour; recreate the bedtime/rush contrast. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: He says the morning post wakes him. His bedtime is our rush hour.

terms.what: The rooftop wind arrow the courier brings to the tallest tower; it spins at the end ("It spins! It points!").
terms.guidance: Weathervane / weathercock. (English takes were checked so it is not heard as "vain/vein".) Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Sorry! I couldn’t look away. And look: the tower’s new weather vane is spinning.

terms.what: The Sky Club's rule and the game's motto: no letter is ever lost. It opens and closes the story, is said by Bill, the courier and the birds, and sits under the logo.
terms.guidance: Translate ONCE as a short punchy slogan and reuse it VERBATIM everywhere (captions, voice, home). "Lands" = arrives/reaches its recipient, and also a bird landing. The Dragon questions it ("Does every letter really land?"): your slogan must work as a question too. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Every letter lands. Got it!

terms.what: The Campaign key's subtitle on Home, a variant of the motto.
terms.guidance: Echo the motto's wording (deliver/land) in a short subtitle.

terms.what: How Postmaster Bill always calls the courier (a beginner on day one); Pip calls himself "Rookie courier Pip" / "Rookie Pip".
terms.guidance: Affectionate word for a newcomer/beginner, informal (Bill uses tu/du); gender-neutral or epicene if possible since it addresses any bird. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: There you are, rookie! Postmaster Bill. Welcome to the Sky Club post.

terms.what: Baron Bat's condescending address to the courier ("This route is my roost now, little courier!").
terms.guidance: Posh condescension; any bird: avoid gendered adjective agreement if possible. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: This route is my roost now, little courier!

terms.what: The Searchlight Gargoyle's catchphrase to everyone (theatrical luvvie), Baron Bat's posh condescension, and one of Peaches's pet names.
terms.guidance: Stage-actor endearment. In gendered languages pick a form usable for any bird (e.g. fr "mon cher/ma chère" is gendered: prefer "mon chou"/"très cher" style neutral options). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: A visitor! Step into the light, darling, let me look at you!

terms.what: The Pirate Captain's slangy word for the courier (a postman).
where: data: Captain's thank-you ("Ye fly well, for a postie.")
terms.guidance: Colloquial "postman"; gender-neutral if possible. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Arr. Ye fly well, for a postie.

terms.what: The Pirate Captain's word for the small courier (a sprat is a tiny fish).
terms.guidance: A sailor's put-down for something small; use a tiny-fish or small-fry word. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Avast! This be the Captain's water, sprat!

terms.what: The Captain's coinage from "landlubber" (a landsman): a creature of the sky.
terms.guidance: Twist your language's pirate insult for landsmen into a sky version. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Me album's got a gap just yer size, skylubber.

terms.what: Pirate address (friend, mate).
terms.guidance: Pirate-speak "buddy". Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Stay out o' the water, matey. She's hungry today.

terms.what: The Pirate Captain calls the courier "lad" in the story; the courier may be any of the four birds.
terms.guidance: GENDER TRAP: "lad" = boy. Use a neutral pirate address (matey, sprat, landlubber equivalent) so it fits Peaches and Orbit too. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Not the mail, lad. The STAMPS. Tiny paper treasure from every port!

terms.what: The Captain's nickname for the courier ("High tide, feathers!").
terms.guidance: A jokey nickname from its feathers. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: High tide, feathers! Fly or swim!

terms.what: The Ember Dragon's address for the courier: a small spark against his fire.
terms.guidance: Keep the fire image; ancient, patronising. Also "Impudent little spark!". Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Your wings are paper, little spark. I am the fire.

terms.what: The Ember Dragon calls the courier a newly hatched bird.
terms.guidance: A just-hatched chick; condescending, ancient. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Fly faster, hatchling. The sky is long, and I am patient.

terms.what: The Dragon's other address ("Deep breath, small one..."); also "messenger", "little bird".
terms.guidance: Neutral for any bird. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Deep breath, small one...

terms.what: The Dusk Empress's lulling address ("Close your eyes, little one."); also "little wanderer", "night bird", "you little ruffian".
terms.guidance: Soft, hushed, gently condescending; neutral for any bird. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Welcome to the dark, little wanderer.

terms.what: Neferhoo's address for the courier (a young bird just learning to fly).
terms.guidance: Fussy-old-man condescension. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: I have outflown sandstorms, fledgling. You are a breeze.

terms.what: Orbit's gentle farewell to Neferhoo.
terms.guidance: Respectful-tender. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Sleep well, old courier. Your letter landed.

terms.what: Bill's affectionate nickname for the Searchlight Gargoyle (a stone face; a poker face).
terms.guidance: A jovial nickname from stone + face; capitalised as a name. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Welcome to the club, Stoneface. And yes, the pigeons may stay.

terms.what: How the courier and Bill address King Coo.
terms.guidance: Same word as title.commissioner. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Commissioner, I remember a bread cart under the theatre marquee, out of the rain.

terms.what: The birds' address for the Spitter King; Pip calls him "His Majesty the beetle".
terms.guidance: Royal address; polite, a little teasing. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Hello, Your Majesty! Please don't boil anybody's letters.

terms.what: Pip bowing to Baron Bat.
terms.guidance: Address for a lord/baron. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: A real Baron! Do I bow? I'm bowing. Your Lordship!

terms.what: Pip on the Dusk Empress.
terms.guidance: Royal third-person reference. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Her Highness! Slip between the fans. Just slip.

terms.what: The courier's polite address to Baron Bat, Neferhoo and King Coo; Peaches even calls a beetle "sir".
terms.guidance: Polite (vous/Sie/usted register, see CHARACTERS.md). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Sir, who is your last letter for?

terms.what: Peaches's cute address ("Hi, Mister Sphinx!", "Go deliver your letter, Mister Neferhoo!", "Return to sender, mister!").
terms.guidance: Childlike politeness ("Mr"). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Go deliver your letter, Mister Neferhoo!

terms.what: Pip and Minty call the player "partner" (the player and bird are a team).
terms.guidance: Buddy/teammate, informal; Minty also says "buddy", "pal" (to enemies), "hotshot" (to himself or the player). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Down I go. We'll get it next time, partner.

terms.what: Peaches's many sugary pet names for the player and even enemies: sweetie, sugar, cupcake, lovebug, gumdrop, buttercup, jellybean, sweet pea, honey, honeybun, sweetheart, darling, sugarplum, pumpkin, poppet, cutie, lovely, fluffy.
terms.guidance: Use your language's affectionate food/sweet pet names, varied (do not repeat one), gender-neutral where possible since the player may be anyone. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Just one heart now. Careful, sweetie, careful.

terms.what: Minty's cheeky nickname for a boss in a retort.
terms.guidance: Pun on boss/bossy. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Words don't fly, bossy. Hummingbirds do!

terms.term: Cousins! / my lovelies / my little scarabs / me hearties
terms.what: How the bosses summon their helpers: Baron Bat "Cousins!", "Relatives!", "my little ones"; the Empress "my lovelies", "my pretties", "my sweets"; the Spitter King "Assistants!", "my little scarabs", "Beetles!"; the Captain "All hands!", "Crew!", "me hearties"; the Dragon "my bats", "shadows of the red sky".
terms.guidance: Plural address in each boss's own register (see CHARACTERS.md). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Rise from the shadows, my pretties.

terms.term: This route is my roost now, little courier!
terms.what: Baron Bat's name-card line (chapter 1, level 1-8 / lair).
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. Posh, peevish; "roost" = where a bat sleeps (his reason: sleep).
terms.example: This route is my roost now, little courier!

terms.term: Every letter on my road goes in the brew!
terms.what: the Spitter King's name-card line (chapter 2, level 2-8 / lair).
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. Mad-alchemist glee; "my road" = chapter.ancient-road, "the brew" = story.brew.
terms.example: Every letter on my road goes in the brew!

terms.term: Hush now. The night mail is sleeping.
terms.what: the Dusk Empress's name-card line (chapter 3, level 3-8 / lair).
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. A hushed lullaby threat; "the night mail" = story.night-mail.
terms.example: Hush now. The night mail is sleeping.

terms.term: Arr! Every mailbag on these waves be mine!
terms.what: the Pirate Captain's name-card line (chapter 4, level 4-8 / lair).
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. Stage-pirate grammar ("be mine" for "are mine"): use your pirate idiom; "mailbag" = story.mailbag.
terms.example: Arr! Every mailbag on these waves be mine!

terms.term: The sky is mine. Your letters are kindling.
terms.what: the Ember Dragon's name-card line (chapter 5, level 5-8 / lair).
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. Grand and cold; "kindling" = story.kindling.
terms.example: The sky is mine. Your letters are kindling.

terms.term: Return to sender! This route has a courier.
terms.what: Neferhoo's guardian name-card line (level 2-6); also `bossLine` in the level data.
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. Opens with his catchphrase (phrase.return-to-sender); "courier" = char.courier.
terms.example: Return to sender! This route has a courier.

terms.term: Nobody flies till the bread cart is found!
terms.what: King Coo's guardian name-card line (level 3-2); also `bossLine` in the level data.
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. A blustering police order; "bread cart" = story.bread-cart.
terms.example: Nobody flies till the bread cart is found!

terms.term: Hold still! Nobody ever stays in the light.
terms.what: the Searchlight Gargoyle's guardian name-card line (level 3-4); also `bossLine` in the level data.
terms.guidance: Shown in quotes on the boss's entrance name card under its epithet, AND spoken as the boss's last line at its lair (story clip, replayed as the card line in flight): caption, card and voice must be word for word the same. A ham actor pleading for an audience; "the light" = his searchlight / the spotlight.
terms.example: Hold still! Nobody ever stays in the light.

terms.what: Neferhoo's catchphrase (the postal stamp on undeliverable mail): he fires his letters, the courier shoots them back to him. Also level 2-6's name, the achievement, the hint, and other characters borrow it (Baron: "Return to sender, darling."; Orbit: "Return to sender, softly.").
where: data: level 2-6 name, hint, boss line
terms.guidance: Use the OFFICIAL postal formula your country's post stamps on returned mail (fr "Retour à l'envoyeur", de "Zurück an den Absender", es "Devuélvase al remitente"…), identical in every use; the prop splits it over two lines (RETURN / TO SENDER). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Return to sender! This route has a courier.

terms.what: Idiom (and song title) for a completed delivery; Neferhoo's gloat, Pip's "Signed, sealed, and exactly on time!", Minty's twist "Signed, sealed, zoomed!".
where: flight voice (neferhoo gloat; pip and minty delivered)
terms.guidance: Use a set phrase for a finished delivery in your language; keep the three-beat rhythm so Minty's twist (last word swapped for a speed word) still works. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Signed, sealed, delivered!

terms.what: Pip's tagline on his bird card; he riffs on it in flight ("Small bird, big sky. Okay!", "Small bird, big plan!").
terms.guidance: A short contrast slogan; reuse its pattern in his riffs. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Look at all that sky. Small bird, big sky. Okay!

terms.term: Rosy cheeks, curly crest, all heart.
terms.what: Peaches's description on her bird card.
terms.guidance: Three-part cute description; "all heart" = very kind.

terms.term: Tiny hummer. Fresh sprig. Full speed.
terms.what: Minty's description on his bird card: a tiny hummingbird ("hummer"), fresh as a sprig of mint, at full speed.
terms.guidance: Three short beats; "hummer" = hummingbird, "sprig" = of mint.

terms.term: A dreamy owl who flies by starlight.
terms.what: Orbit's description on her bird card; Bill also says "Fly by starlight, rookie."
terms.guidance: Gentle; same "by starlight" wording as Bill's line. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: I’d bet my cap she has one. Fly by starlight, rookie.

terms.what: One of the four shared sprint calls every bird shouts when it sprints (story voice clips sprint-<bird>-*, played in flight too).
terms.guidance: A joyful whoop. One or two words, exclamatory; the SAME text is voiced by all four birds, so it must not be gendered. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Woo-hooo!

terms.what: One of the four shared sprint calls every bird shouts when it sprints (story voice clips sprint-<bird>-*, played in flight too).
terms.guidance: Comic: feathers with a turbo boost. One or two words, exclamatory; the SAME text is voiced by all four birds, so it must not be gendered. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Turbo feathers!

terms.what: One of the four shared sprint calls every bird shouts when it sprints (story voice clips sprint-<bird>-*, played in flight too).
terms.guidance: Waving gravity goodbye. One or two words, exclamatory; the SAME text is voiced by all four birds, so it must not be gendered. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Bye-bye, gravity!

terms.what: One of the four shared sprint calls every bird shouts when it sprints (story voice clips sprint-<bird>-*, played in flight too).
terms.guidance: A joyful "whee" of speed. One or two words, exclamatory; the SAME text is voiced by all four birds, so it must not be gendered. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Wheeee!

terms.what: Bill's encouragement (like "chin up"); Pip quotes it on his last heart.
terms.guidance: Bird version of "keep your chin up"; use your idiom with beak instead of chin/head. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Keep your beak up. Postmaster's orders. Beak... up.

terms.what: Bill on Baron Bat: like "all bark and no bite".
where: flight voice (pip: "He's all screech, Bill says.")
terms.guidance: Recreate "all bark, no bite" with a bat's screech. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: He’s all screech, rookie. Dodge the fireballs and shoot back!

terms.term: No flame seal on this guardian.
terms.what: Bill's line at Neferhoo's and King Coo's lairs: guardians are not part of the trail of seals.
terms.guidance: Same wording both times; "flame seal" = story.flame-seal, "guardian" = ui.guardian. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: No flame seal on this guardian. Just a hungry pigeon and his star-grabbing gang.

terms.what: The guardians' stop order: Neferhoo and King Coo both open with it.
terms.guidance: Military/police "Stop!", shouted, all caps. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: HALT! By order of the Commissioner, nothing with wheels or wings passes!

terms.what: Baron Bat's pun on "No more Mister Nice Guy" when he gets angry.

terms.guidance: Keep "look up" consistent across both scenes; it is the emotional payoff. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Ninety-odd years on this ledge. Everyone admires the skyline. Nobody looks up.

terms.what: King Coo and the Searchlight Gargoyle accept their club jobs speaking of themselves in the third person ("…The Gargoyle accepts.").
terms.guidance: Keep the pompous third-person formula in both lines. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: A bagel a day? …The Commissioner accepts.

terms.what: A piece of mail: the heart of the game ("Every letter lands."). Bosses steal, boil, burn or keep letters; the last delivery is a letter to the Dragon.
terms.guidance: The postal sense (a written message in an envelope), never the alphabet sense, EXCEPT in two jokes: Bill's "He dotted his “i” with a tiny bat." and the Spitter King boiling "the words right off the page". Use one word for letter everywhere, the same as in the motto. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: One letter, and it’s for you. It says: stop boiling the post.

terms.what: Two words the English uses for the same thing: "mail" (letters and parcels: "Where does the mail go?", "mailbag", "night mail") and "post" (the postal service and its deliveries, British: "the Sky Club post", "the morning post", "the Pharaoh's post", "stop boiling the post", "POST!"). Postman/postie = mail carrier.
terms.guidance: Your language may have one word for both. Keep fixed compounds stable: Sky Club post (ui.sky-club-post), night mail (story.night-mail), morning post (story.morning-post), mailbag (story.mailbag), the Pharaoh's post (story.pharaohs-post). "postman" (Bill on Neferhoo, the Baron's "Sunrise is for pigeons and postmen.") is the ordinary mail-carrier word. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Ready to fly! Where does the mail go?

terms.what: A package; every level's cargo is a parcel or letter ("A wire can't carry a parcel, rookie. Or a hug. Or noodles.").
terms.guidance: Postal parcel/package. Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: A wire can’t carry a parcel, rookie. Or a hug. Or noodles.

terms.what: Handing mail to its recipient; "deliver", "delivered", "special delivery", "First Delivery" (1-1). The courier's whole job.
terms.guidance: Postal delivery; keep the verb and noun from the same root where your language allows (deliver / delivery / delivered). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: Four thousand years late. Not my finest delivery.

terms.what: The letter salutations: the club's letter to the Ember Dragon opens "Dear Dragon." and each chapter postcard opens "Dear courier,".
terms.guidance: Your normal letter salutation ("Cher/Chère…", "Liebe/r…", "Querido/a…"): pick a form that fits any bird (the courier) and the Dragon (masculine). Spoken in voice lines: captions, UI and voice must use the same wording.
terms.example: “Dear Dragon. The Sky Club has a new route, and no one to light the way.”
